1         III.     LARGE LOAD TARIFFS, ESA AND CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS

2                                             A. OVERVIEW

3    Q7.         WHAT PARTIES HAVE FILED TESTIMONY ADDRESSING EPE’S

4                PROPOSED NEW RATE OFFERINGS AND TERMS FOR SERVING

5                LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS?

6    A.          Commission Staff and the following intervenors filed Direct Testimony addressing

7                and recommending changes to portions of EPE’s proposed large load tariffs (Rate

8                50 and Rate 51). Other parties included: Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy

9                (CCAE), City of Las Cruces (CLC), Doña Ana County (DAC), New Mexico

10               Department of Justice (NMDOJ), New Mexico State University (NMSU), and

11               United States Department of Defense/Federal Executive Agencies (DoD/FEA).

12

13   Q8.         WHAT ARE THE PRIMARY DRIVERS FOR EPE’S PROPOSAL FOR A

14               SEPARATE TARIFF TO SERVE LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS IN THIS

15               RATE CASE?

16   A.          EPE’s existing Rate No. 09 was not designed for customers of the magnitude or

17               characteristics EPE is now being asked to consider. As I explained in my Direct

18               Testimony, the largest customer currently served under Rate No. 09 has a peak

19               demand below 10 MW, and the class has an average load factor of approximately

20               60 percent. The customers contemplated by EPE's proposed large-load tariffs can

21               be substantially larger and may have very different operating characteristics and

                                                     6
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      GEORGE NOVELA

1          require substantially large build-out to serve. EPE has concluded that simply

2          placing those types of customers on an existing tariff, such as Rate No. 09, would

3          not appropriately recognize their potentially different costs and risks. That is why

4          EPE has proposed Rate No. 50 for customers at or above 30 MW with high load

5          factors and Rate No. 51 beginning at 10 MW.

6

7    Q9.   DO    STAFF AND INTERVENORS                   GENERALLY SUPPORT                 THE

8          CONCEPT OF A SEPARATE RATE OFFERING TO SERVE LARGE

9          CUSTOMERS?

10   A.    Yes. Staff and intervenors generally support separate tariffs that target large-loads.

11         For example, Staff witness Douglas Jester expressly agrees that a separate tariff for

12         unusually large-loads is necessary to manage risks and cost impacts on other

13         customers and agrees that a 10 MW threshold for Rate No. 51 is appropriate.

14         Likewise, CCAE witness Ron Nelson acknowledges that EPE's proposals are a step

15         in the right direction. Importantly, these parties have recognized that EPE

16         appropriately identified the large-load issue and proactively developed a structure

17         to address it. This substantial agreement should not be overlooked.

18

19   Q10. WHAT ARE STAFF AND INTERVENORS’ PRIMARY CONCERNS WITH

20         EPE’S PROPOSAL?




                                                 7
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1    A.   The focus of Staff and intervenor Direct Testimonies on this issue is largely whether

2         EPE’s proposal goes far enough to protect non-large load customers. Intervenors

3         also raise concern with existing customers being involuntarily moved to the

4         proposed large load rates.

5

6          B. ENERGY SERVICE AGREEMENT AND TARIFF PROVISIONS

7    Q11. PLEASE DESCRIBE EPE'S PROPOSAL FOR LARGE LOAD TARIFFS.

8    A.   EPE proposed the Original Rate No. 50 – High Load Factor Service Rate (“Rate

9         50”) and the Original Rate No. 51 – Large Load Service Rate (“Rate 51”)

10        (collectively, “Large Load”) tariff schedules specifically to address the advent of

11        large-load customers and protect existing customers against inappropriate cost

12        shifting. These proposed rates, developed and presented by Mr. Carrasco in his

13        Direct Testimony, reflect a full cost of service and ratemaking analysis based on

14        information from EPE’s cost of service study. While the resulting rates are lower

15        than existing Schedule No. 09 levels, they are not discounted. They are cost-based

16        and reflect the same jurisdictional costs and cost allocation principles underlying

17        EPE’s current retail rates for all other customers, as well as the unique (both high

18        and low load factor) characteristics of large-load customers.

19               The proposed Large Load tariff schedules will be applicable for new

20        customers in targeted business sectors with minimum monthly billing demand of at

21        least 30 MW (for Rate 50) or 10 MW (for Rate 51), who would otherwise qualify


                                                8
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         for service under EPE’s Schedule No. 09 (among other schedules for large

2         customers). A customer qualifies for these schedules as a large load under these

3         requirements. As described by Mr. Carrasco in his testimony, EPE provides an

4         option for large-load customers with either a high or a low load factor. The

5         proposed Large Load tariff schedules, require a large-load customer to execute an

6         Energy Service Agreement (“ESA”) with EPE that must be filed with the

7         Commission before taking service under the rate. I have included an example ESA

8         as Exhibit GN-2 to my Direct Testimony. Section 10 of the sample agreement is a

9         placeholder for any additional terms and conditions that may be necessary or

10        specific to a customer.

11

12   Q12. WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THE ESA AND IS EPE REQUESTING THE

13        COMMISSION TO APPROVE EACH ESA GOING FORWARD?

14   A.   EPE's proposal should be evaluated as an integrated package rather than by

15        examining one tariff provision in isolation. The framework combines specialized

16        large load tariffs described above with a customer-specific ESA. If approved, the

17        terms of the ESA are required to be incorporated and be consistent with the Large

18        Load tariff rates, terms and conditions to ensure that the large load customer’s

19        financial commitment covers EPE’s investment in the facilities necessary to

20        provide them with service while contemporaneously protecting EPE’s other

21        customers. The required ESA terms, set forth in the Large Load tariff rates, include

                                               9
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         the following customer protection measures: minimum billing obligations, long-

2         term contractual commitments, financial security, dedicated-facility cost recovery,

3         termination damages, load-ramp provisions, technical requirements. This Large

4         Load tariff ESA framework provides EPE the flexibility to negotiate terms with

5         each applicable customer where service terms and requirements may vastly differ,

6         which I address in more detail below. EPE requests that the Commission open a

7         new Rate No. 50 and Rate No. 51 compliance docket for the purpose of filing

8         executed ESAs. Within a reasonable time following execution, EPE will cause the

9         ESA to be filed and served through PRC e360 on counsel of record and pro se

10        parties to EPE’s last general rate case. While EPE has not stated in this proceeding

11        that it plans to seek explicit Commission approval for each ESA, the Commission’s

12        ratemaking authority extends to all filed ESAs and EPE would seek approval as

13        required.

14

15   Q13. PLEASE PROVIDE ADDITIONAL SUPPORT FOR THE LARGE LOAD

16        TARIFF ESA FRAMEWORK.

17   A.   Individual large-load projects may differ considerably in size, operating

18        characteristics, creditworthiness, load ramp, and infrastructure requirements.

19        Therefore, the precise contractual terms may appropriately vary to address

20        legitimate project-specific circumstances. Those differences do not mean that EPE




                                               10
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         would be able to abandon the underlying customer protections set forth in the large

2         load tariffs.

3                 Under EPE’s proposed framework, the Commission retains complete

4         oversight of future ESAs. Each ESA must conform to Rate No. 50 or Rate No. 51

5         as ultimately approved by the Commission, and the Commission should retain

6         discretion to order a contested case concerning an ESA for a new or expanded large-

7         load customer, either on its own motion or upon petition by an interested party.

8         This approach preserves Commission oversight and the fundamental protections

9         for existing customers while allowing reasonable project-specific flexibility in an

10        individual ESA.

11

12   Q14. IS EPE PROPOSING TO MODIFY ITS PROPOSED LARGE LOAD

13        TARIFFS OR ILLUSTRATIVE ENERGY SERVICE AGREEMENT IN

14        RESPONSE TO PARTIES’ RECOMMENDATIONS?

15   A.   Yes. EPE is proposing changes to the applicability of the tariffs. EPE has proposed

16        to require a customer otherwise eligible for Rate No. 09 that exceeds the 10 MW

17        threshold to take service under the applicable large-load rate if it meets the

18        eligibility requirements of Rate No. 50 or Rate No. 51. However, in response to

19        DOD/FEA and NMSU Direct Testimony, EPE agrees to include an exception to

20        the applicability section that the 10 MW limitation does not apply to customers

21        eligible for service under another dedicated or customer-specific rate schedule. For


                                               11
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    GEORGE NOVELA

1         example, existing military customers and NMSU remain eligible for service under

2         their applicable dedicated schedules and are not required to migrate to Rate Nos.

3         50 or 51 solely because their annual peak demand exceeds 10 MW. EPE agrees

4         this modification preserves the purpose of EPE's large-load proposal while avoiding

5         unintended changes to existing Commission-approved rate arrangements. I will

6         discuss this change in more detail below.

7

8    Q15. STAFF CHARACTERIZES EPE'S PROPOSED LARGE-LOAD TARIFFS

9         AS INADEQUATE. DO YOU AGREE?

10   A.   No. EPE's proposal should be evaluated as an integrated package rather than by

11        examining one tariff provision in isolation. The framework combines specialized

12        large-load tariffs that require minimum billing obligations, long-term contractual

13        commitments, financial security, dedicated-facility cost recovery, termination

14        damages, load-ramp provisions, technical requirements, and customer-specific

15        ESAs. These are meaningful protections specifically designed to address the risk

16        that a very large customer does not develop or remain on EPE's system as initially

17        anticipated, and each will be incorporated into a customer specific ESA which will

18        be filed with the Commission.

19

20   Q16. STAFF WITNESS JESTER’S DIRECT TESTIMONY TAKES ISSUE WITH

21        EPE’S ASSESSMENT OF THE RISK LARGE-LOAD PRESENTS TO

                                              12
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         EXISTING CUSTOMERS. DID EPE CONSIDER THIS ISSUE IN

2         DEVELOPING THE PROPOSAL?

3    A.   Yes. As stated above, this is a key basis for EPE's proposal. Rate Nos. 50 and 51

4         were specifically designed to introduce cost-shifting protections associated with the

5         advent of large-load customers. Accordingly, EPE agrees with Staff witness Jester

6         and CCAE witness Nelson on the fundamental regulatory objective: existing

7         customers should be appropriately protected from risks created by extraordinarily

8         large new loads. Where EPE disagrees is with the suggestion that achieving that

9         objective requires rejection of EPE's proposed framework and replacement with

10        their preferred, prescriptive tariff terms, as I address in more detail below.

11

12   Q17. STAFF WITNESS JESTER RECOMMENDS THAT LARGE-LOAD

13        CUSTOMERS PRIMARILY BE DIRECTLY ASSIGNED THE COST OF

14        INCREMENTAL RESOURCES NECESSARY TO SERVE THEM. WHAT

15        IS YOUR RESPONSE?

16   A.   I agree with the general cost-causation principle, but I disagree that Staff has

17        demonstrated a reasonable basis to adopt its proposed direct-assignment model in

18        place of EPE's proposal. Staff’s proposal directly assigns incremental resources to

19        the large-load customer, while also requiring the customer to pay a share of

20        common resources and overhead. Staff then proposes to have EPE demonstrate for

21        each ESA that the large-load customer pays all costs caused by it and produces at

                                                13
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    GEORGE NOVELA

1         least a modest reduction in costs allocated to existing customers. There is a

2         considerable conceptual agreement between EPE and Staff’s proposals to protect

3         existing customers against cost shifting. The difference is that EPE accomplishes

4         that objective through an integrated combination of tariff rates, including line-

5         extension requirements, facility-specific charges, financial security, minimum

6         billing obligations, long-term contracts, and termination protection. The fact that

7         Staff’s witness has presented a different way to structure the protections is not a

8         reasonable basis to deny EPE’s proposal.

9

10   Q18. CCAE WITNESS NELSON ARGUES THAT EPE'S MINIMUM BILL

11        SHOULD INCLUDE A MINIMUM ENERGY VOLUME. DO YOU AGREE?

12   A.   I do not agree that a minimum energy requirement has been shown to be necessary

13        in addition to EPE's existing protections. The proposed tariffs already provide a

14        substantial minimum billing-demand obligation. CCAE witness Nelson

15        acknowledges that the contemplated billing-demand definition can include 80

16        percent of Contract Capacity, an 80 percent demand ratchet based on summer

17        demand and, for Rate No. 50, a 30 MW floor. That demand-based minimum,

18        together with the ESA's Facility Charge, security provisions, long contractual term

19        and termination damages, provides substantial protection against a customer

20        receiving the benefit of system investment while materially reducing its financial

21        contribution. Adding a separate minimum-energy requirement should therefore

                                              14
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    GEORGE NOVELA

1         require a demonstration that the existing mechanisms leave a material unrecovered

2         exposure, not simply that another jurisdiction has adopted a different contractual

3         structure.

4

5    Q19. DO      YOU       AGREE        WITH        STAFF       WITNESS         JESTER'S

6         RECOMMENDATION TO LIMIT RATE NO. 09 TO CUSTOMERS WITH

7         AN ANNUAL PEAK DEMAND THAT DOES NOT EXCEED 10 MW?

8    A.   Yes, subject to an exception for customers on dedicated or customer-specific rate

9         schedules.

10

11   Q20. DO YOU AGREE WITH NMSU WITNESS MICHAEL GORMAN AND

12        DOD/FEA WITNESS LARRY BLANK’S RECOMMENDATION TO

13        ALLOW EXISTING CUSTOMERS WHO WOULD QUALIFY FOR RATE

14        NOS. 50 AND 51 TO REMAIN ON THEIR CURRENT RATE SCHEDULES?

15   A.   Yes, with clarification. As mentioned above EPE agrees that customers currently

16        taking service under an existing Commission-approved dedicated or customer-

17        specific rate schedule should generally be permitted to remain on that schedule for

18        their existing load. Rate Nos. 50 and 51 are intended principally to address new or

19        expanded large-loads and the additional costs and risks associated with serving

20        those loads. Accordingly, an existing customer should not be required to migrate

21        its existing load to Rate No. 50 or Rate No. 51 solely because its demand may

                                              15
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         satisfy one of the large-load thresholds. For example, NMSU's existing load may

2         continue to take service under Rate No. 26.

3

4    Q21. WOULD THAT EXCEPTION UNDERMINE THE PURPOSE OF RATE

5         NOS. 50 AND 51?

6    A.   No. Rate Nos. 50 and 51 would continue to apply to customers that satisfy the

7         applicable eligibility requirements and do not otherwise qualify for service under a

8         dedicated rate schedule. The clarification simply recognizes that the 10 MW

9         threshold should determine whether a customer, otherwise taking general large-

10        power service under Rate No. 09, should instead take service under EPE's large-

11        load tariffs. It should not displace rate schedules that were specifically established

12        for customers such as military installations or NMSU.

13

14                             C. CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS

15   Q22. STAFF WITNESS JESTER POINTS OUT THAT EPE COULD RECEIVE A

16        REQUEST FROM A CUSTOMER MUCH LARGER THAN THE

17        HYPOTHETICAL CUSTOMERS USED IN ITS ANALYSIS. DOES THAT

18        OBSERVATION SUPPORT DENYING RATE NOS. 50 AND 51?

19   A.   No. In my view, it demonstrates why EPE needs a large-load framework. EPE's

20        proposed large load tariffs establish the governing framework, while the ESA

21        addresses the specific customer's circumstances, including contract capacity, load

                                               16
                                    EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                    REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                        GEORGE NOVELA

1         ramp, facilities, financial security, technical requirements and other customer-

2         specific terms. For example, the ESA expressly does not grant the customer a

3         reservation of capacity or priority over other EPE customers, and the customer

4         cannot increase its connected load above its applicable contract capacity. The

5         possibility that future customers may vary greatly in size does not establish that

6         EPE should have no approved large load tariff until every possible configuration

7         has been anticipated. The ESA is structured to allow for and address such variations

8         within the class.

9

10   Q23. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF’S RECOMMENDATION TO ORDER EPE

11        TO FILE ITS PROPOSAL IN A SEPARATE DOCKET RATHER THAN

12        DECIDING THIS MATTER IN THIS PROCEEDING?

13   A.   No. Doing so would leave unresolved the very regulatory gap all parties recognize.

14        The parties generally agree with EPE’s objective to implement a separate tariff for

15        service of very large loads that includes protections for other customers before very

16        large customers began taking service. Staff agrees that unusually large loads

17        require a separate tariff and that a 10 MW eligibility threshold is appropriate. EPE’s

18        proposal presents a comprehensive structure specifically intended to meet that

19        objective. Specifically, EPE's proposal establishes dedicated Rate Nos. 50 and 51

20        and the requirement for a customer-specific ESA, provides a long-term contractual

21        commitment,         establishes   minimum-billing   obligations,   financial-security

                                                 17
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     GEORGE NOVELA

1         provisions, customer-specific Facility Charges, termination protection, load-ramp

2         requirements and technical conditions, and is accompanied by significant changes

3         to EPE's Line Extension Policy. The Commission should not reject the proposal in

4         its entirety simply because parties like Staff or CCAE would design it differently.

5         The Commission should approve EPE's proposal as a reasonable and proactive first

6         step for serving future large-loads while protecting other New Mexico customers.

7

8    Q24. CCAE      WITNESS       NELSON        CONTENDS         THAT      TRADITIONAL

9         EMBEDDED COST RATEMAKING COULD SHIFT THE COST OF

10        LARGE-LOADS TO EXISTING CUSTOMERS. DOES EPE AGREE WITH

11        THIS CONCERN?

12   A.   No. Mr. Nelson's criticism focuses heavily on comparing embedded and

13        incremental cost allocation. He argues that where the incremental cost of serving a

14        new customer exceeds embedded system costs, traditional embedded allocation

15        may cause existing customers to bear part of that incremental cost. But EPE is not

16        proposing simply to place these customers into its traditional Rate No. 09 structure

17        and rely exclusively on ordinary embedded-cost rates. EPE developed Rate Nos.

18        50 and 51 precisely because the existing tariff structure was not considered

19        adequate for customers above 10 MW with these characteristics. EPE's ESA further

20        provides for the customer's Facility Charge, security, minimum-charge and

21        termination obligations. The Facility Charge includes a return of and on EPE's
